speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas recently released figures show the government spent in a few days nearly $803 million of our U.S. dollar reserves supporting the falling Canadian dollar, but those figures do not include the final day of transactions in November, net future forward positions and the impact of our chartered banks losing $925 million in their net foreign currency assets in recent weeks, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):

Turner, a subsequent Minister of Finance, following a dollar decline of minor importance in terms of reserve spending compared to our reserve outflow of recent weeks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of the difficulties currently being experienced by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts in investigating the events surrounding the sale of nuclear reactors to South Korea and Argentina, and in light of the fact that much of this
difficulty arises from the unwillingness of the government to provide the committee with adequate documentation with regard to these events, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government be instructed to transmit to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts as soon as possible the minutes of AECL meetings of the directors at which these sales were discussed; copies of all contracts and correspondence between AECL and Shaul Eisenberg or any of his companies; all contracts signed for the sale of such reactors to date; and all correspondence between AECL and its Italian partner in the sale of a nuclear reactor to Argentina.

subsubtopic: BEEF-POSSIBILITY OF BILATERAL ARRANGEMENT WITH UNITED STATES ON IMPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture relating to current beef import negotiations in Washington involving most of the major beef exporting countries to the United States. In view of the fact that Canada appears to be somewhat reluctant to enter into these negotiations and in view of the status of the temporary quotas now imposed by both Canada and the United States, will the minister tell us whether Canada is asking for some special bilateral arrangement between ourselves and the United States? If so, will such arrangements ensure continued two-way fair trade in beef between Canada and the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: BEEF-POSSIBILITY OF BILATERAL ARRANGEMENT WITH UNITED STATES ON IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many products are traded between United States and Canada,
Oral Questions
not just beef, differently than with other countries. However, we think we may have to have a different kind of arrangement for this kind of trading to continue. We thought we had made an arrangement about a year ago in beef trade between the United States and Canada; agreement was reached between the former secretary of agriculture and myself, a voluntary arrangement under which when our trade becomes exorbitant to them or their trade becomes exorbitant to us so far as beef is concerned we would notify one another. That procedure was not followed and they did not notify us. In the interval the President of the United States introduced the new import law, so we feel we were not treated in the way that we agreed upon.
We are still in negotiation with the United States at the present time. Whether we are going to come up with some mutually agreed, voluntary type of agreement, I do not know, but I am not too happy with voluntary types of agreements made verbally. The same thing happened to us with Australia and New Zealand; a verbal agreement was entered into with them on the pricing of beef into Canada to the effect that it would not be priced more than six cents below the price in the United States. I am sure the hon. member knows that they sold beef into Canada as much as 39 cents a pound less than they sold to the United States. Consumers never had much of the benefit and it caused a disruption of the normal marketings of meat in Canada. So, I do not look too kindly on verbal agreements.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the very obvious problems brought on throughout all of 1976 by offshore beef imports from Australia and New Zealand and correspondingly heavy exports of our cows and beef to the United States, would the minister indicate whether separate negotiations are also underway with respect to these offshore imports so as to restore such beef imports to reasonable, historical levels effective the first of 1977 by using, if necessary, a Canadian meat import law, since our Export and Import Permits Act does not seem to do the job, especially when we need prompt action?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
This is our concern, Mr. Speaker. The United States of America, Australia and New Zealand are members of GATT, as is Canada. In addition, Australia and New Zealand are fellow members of the Commonwealth. We have trading agreements in the Commonwealth giving preferential treatment to our Commonwealth partners. So it is difficult to say that we will treat Australia and New Zealand differently from the United States of America. Even if we think the situation is a little different, one has to consider all these things when one is trying to make a proper trading arrangement. If we are going to have a hidebound written agreement with Australia and New Zealand on pricing and on how much is imported into Canada, it will be difficult to have a different arrangement with the United States of America and that is our problem. We are

December 10,1976

trying to solve the problem and are taking a friendly attitude, but as I have said, my past experience with the United States and with Australia and New Zealand has not been pleasant so far as their living up to verbal agreements is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises out of a series of answers given by the Minister of Finance with regard to Canadian international monetary exchange activities in the past few days. I raise this question of privilege because hon. members of the House of Commons ask questions which they consider to be significant, and expect and count on the fact that when answers are given people across Canada can rely on those answers in making very important decisions.
On November 30, 1976, the minister said, as reported at page 1498 of Hansard, in reply to a question about the activities of the Bank of Canada in the exchange market, "we would accept to let the Canadian currency go to whatever level international trading would take it". Obviously, many significant Canadian investors had a decision to make with respect to how to deal with the Canadian dollar. The figures are now out, and it is quite apparent that there was massive intervention by the Bank of Canada to support the dollar at a certain level. I raise this matter only to find out whether the minister would be prepared this weekend, or in the House, to make a clarification of what is clearly a contradictory situation, so that people involved in international trading can rely on the information elicited in the House of Commons as being an accurate reflection of the policy of the government.

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF PREVENTING CLOSING OF DOMTAR PLANT AT GEORGETOWN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it does not seem to me that there is any substantial point, either of privilege or of substance, raised by the intervention of the hon. member. As the House knows, and as has been long-standing practice as stated by successive governors of the Bank of Canada and as supported in that respect by successive ministers of finance, the Canadian dollar being in a floating position, the government of Canada through the Bank of Canada would not intervene for the purpose of holding it at any particular value.
At the same time, the position has been taken that given the erratic nature of the international market in currency, the Bank of Canada should intervene from time to time to smooth out transactions which would occur while not counteracting the direction in which the currency is being taken at a particular period of time. The hon. member for Don Valley knows that very well; certainly, the money market generally knows that very well, and I would regard any suggestion otherwise as being mischievous.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Is the government giving consideration to exempting money obtained from the sale of farm lands from capital gains tax if the money is reinvested in similar property for the purpose of farming within three years?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: It would be difficult to justify such exemptions to farmers without extending similar treatment to other businessmen who may wish to expand or relocate their businesses. Taxation of capital gains is essential if we are to have an income tax system which is genuinely equitable among taxpayers. The exclusion of capital gains from the tax base discriminates unfairly between the person who receives part of his income as capital gains and the man who derives the same amount from taxable sources, such as wages. Since a farmer earns income from his farmland in a way similar to any businessman earning income from the use of his capital assets, it is appropriate to apply capital gains tax on the increase in value when such income-producing assets are sold. Any change in this system to exempt gains reinvested in farmland would treat farmers much more favourably than others on the voluntary disposition of property and reinvestment of proceeds. It would create a preferential precedent and would not likely be acceptable to a majority of Canadians. It should also be pointed out that farmers are the only group that enjoy a special capital gains tax deferral on an intergenerational transfer of farm property, whether that transfer is by way of bequest or inter-vivos sale.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
that Bill C-7, respecting the administration and development of certain fishing and recreational harbours in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to present for second reading Bill C-7, the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act. A new act is required to give the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment the necessary legislative authority to develop and administer the commercial fishing and recreational boat harbours in Canada so as to meet the changing requirements of the commercial fisheries and the growing needs of sports fishing and recreational boating. There are some 2,300 of these small harbours and wharves located across the country, with some ports comprising several wharves and other marine facilities.

Mr. Speaker, legislative authority for the administration of these ports is now granted under the Government Harbours and Piers Act and the accompanying government Wharf Regulations. The act, which dates back to 1895 and was revised in 1937, is mostly regulatory and is not flexible enough to be adapted to modern technology and the development requirements of fishing and recreational harbours.
The clauses of Bill C-7 concerning expansion provide for an extended choice of measures through which we shall be able to come to the best possible arrangements, which will enable us

December 10, 1976

to meet as best as possible requirements for commercial fishing and recreational harbours. These clauses offer more flexibility in the choice of types of programs which will be needed in the future to meet changes. This is seriously lacking under the present legislation. I would like to speak further on this question since it concerns the projects that we would like to suggest after this legislation is passed.
Commercial fishing is an important industry in the Canadian economy. This industry concerns about 38,000 fishing vessels which employ more than 77,000 men and women if we count the fish processing sector, and pumps more than $700 million a year into our economy, including $400 million from exports. The industry has an especially important role to play in the economy of the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia. For these reasons, the government must continue to be concerned about the welfare of commercial fishermen in the Canadian fishing industry.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: Does that include Eagle River?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Yes. One of the essential elements of a prosperous fishing industry is of course the development of a sufficient number of ports and port facilities, well located in fishing zones and of maximum quality. The government will therefore continue to build, maintain and administer these ports by giving priority to these operations when allocating budgetary funds.
More specifically, this includes first the planning and development of a national network of fishing harbours under policies and provisions put forward to meet the changing and diversified needs of the fishing industry in Canada. Second, the repairing, maintenance, extension and upgrading of existing facilities and the creation of new ones. Third, the operation of such facilities; and finally, the continuous management of the network, both nationally and regionally.

The general rise in the Canadian standard of living over the past two decades has contributed to increased and widespread recreational activity. This, in turn, has stimulated the growth of secondary industries such as recreational boat building and the manufacture of related equipment. In 1974 there were approximately 800,000 Canadian-based pleasure craft and 70,000 tourist craft visiting Canada from abroad. It is estimated that these numbers may increase by at least 50 per cent by the end of the 1970s. Neither the private nor the public sector is adequately meeting this rapid increase in demand for marinas and launching ramps catering to recreational boating.
As a result, the proliferation of recreational boats has caused acute congestion in many parts of the country, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia where the bulk of the recreational boating activity is concentrated. In many cases this congestion represents a hazard to life and property, adds to the pollution and threatens to despoil the natural scenic attractions of the environment. Although we are conscious of the fact that outdoor recreational activity and preservation of the environment are of great concern to all levels of govern-
Fishing and Recreational Harbours ment, we recognize the very special interests of the provinces and municipalities in these areas. Our policies in regard to the provision of harbours and associated facilities for recreational boating, such as marinas and launching ramps, will therefore be directed toward promoting development, rather than the direct involvement which I have described in the case of the fishing harbours. Programs will emphasize joint planning and co-operation with the provinces so as to provide a national system of harbours which will meet the needs of recreational boaters with minimum disruption of the environment. Construction, operation and maintenance of facilities providing access to the water, such as launching ramps, will be primarily the concern of provincial and municipal levels of government. We will be proposing some cost-sharing arrangements to encourage this type of development.
In the area of administration, the bill contains enabling provisions to lease property, which will allow the minister to manage and maintain harbours under his jurisdiction, to make and enforce regulations and to prescribe and collect charges for the use of the harbours. Within this consolidated authority we will be introducing a number of new innovations to improve the administration of harbour facilities. For example, under the Government Harbours and Piers Act the minister is restricted in the leasing of wharves to any provincial government, municipal council, harbour commission, shipping company or railway company. As an example, recently we received a request from the Sans Souci and Copperhead Association in Ontario, supported by the local member of parliament, to lease the Sans Souci wharf. This area has no municipal government and, therefore, the wharf could not be leased to the association under the authority of the Government Harbours and Piers Act, even though this was a very legitimate and worth-while proposal. Answers to this type of situation are provided for within the enabling provisions of Bill C-7 and should not arise in the future once this legislation is in force.
At the present time, the majority of our harbours and wharves have no day-to-day supervision but are managed directly by the small craft harbours regional managers in each region. A small number of locations, about 200, have wharfingers who are appointed by the minister "at pleasure" and derive their remuneration from the berthage fees they collect. Their authority to enforce regulations is minimal and is based on procedures which are, at best, cumbersome. Such a system, combined with an inadequate fee structure, has resulted in ineffective and spotty management. I intend to introduce an improved management system which will be flexible and responsive to the needs of the fishermen. Harbour managers will be given the authority required to properly manage their harbours and facilities, and will be provided by the regulations with adequate means of enforcement.
Charges for berthing as now prescribed under the Government Harbours and Piers Act have resulted in many problems due primarily, but not solely, to the failure to recognize the difference in the nature of the fisheries between the various regions of the country. For example, no charges are presently levied against commercial fishing vessels under 45 feet in the

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours Atlantic fishing areas and, in general, charges are not collected in a consistent and equitable manner across the country. The fishing and recreational harbours act will enable us to introduce a new system of harbour mooring fees which will be sensitive to market demand, will recognize regional differences and relate to the level and quality of services provided. Moreover, I hope to change the present inequitable method of collection to include a simplified fee structure including, where possible, an annual or seasonal charge which will permit vessels to berth at any federally-owned facility without additional charge.
I have outlined, Mr. Speaker, the philosophy and main enabling provisions of this bill to provide legislative authority for the development, maintenance and administration of fishing and recreational harbours. At the risk of repeating myself, I would like to conclude with an observation. The promotion of a vigorous and efficient commercial fishery in Canada is an important goal of this government. To achieve this goal requires a variety of policies and programs, including the provision of adequate and properly managed harbours, so as to give the industry and the fishermen the harbours they need when and where they are needed.
Mr. Speaker, I recommend this bill to the hon. members of this House. I readily recognize that discussions in committee can lead to positive and useful suggestions.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-7 entitled "an act respecting the administration and development of certain fishing and recreational harbours in Canada." This bill, on the surface, would appear to be nothing more than a housekeeping bill, a bill which transfers from the Department of Public Works and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) administra-

tive responsibility to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment. However, upon close examination I cannot help noting that this bill adds still further financial burdens to an already over-burdened fishing industry. I understand-and I am supported by the minister's statement of this morning- that legislative authority for administration of our small craft harbours was provided by the Government Harbours and Piers Act and its accompanying wharf regulations, as well as various orders in council. Because it was drafted in 1895 and revised in 1937, the act does not focus on the present-day administrative needs of fishermen and recreational boaters and does not include provision for the development of these harbours.
It is interesting to note that when programs and administrative responsibilities for these harbours were transferred to the Department of Fisheries from the Department of Public Works and the Minister of Transport in June, 1973, the transfer was brought about by order in council. Obviously, our fisheries interests have suffered because the minister's authority over small craft harbours has been derived from an order in council rather than from a legislative enactment. I am informed that one Transport official actually refused to acknowledge the transfer and sent his files to the minister a little more than a month ago. The interpretation clause of this bill reads in part:
"scheduled harbour" means any fishing or recreational harbour included in a schedule prescribed by the regulations.
That definition covers any harbour, wharf, pier, breakwater, slipway, marina or part thereof, together with machinery, works, land and structures related or attached thereto, and any other facility, installation, work or part thereof located on or adjacent to water. That is a tall order, Mr. Speaker. When we examine the regulations included in the bill to see what it meant by a scheduled harbour, we learn, as set out in clause 9:
The governor in council may make regulations (a) prescribing schedules naming and delimiting or describing the fishing or recreational harbours that are under the control and administration of the minister for the purposes of this act-
It can readily be seen from the wording of the bill that the minister has been granted wide powers, and although we are not opposing this legislation, we would be remiss in our duty if we failed to register our concern over the wording of some parts of this bill. For example, the budget for small craft harbours this year is in the order of $35 million. Some of this money will be used for repair and modernization of government fishing wharves on the east coast.
As the minister has stated, there are some 2,300 government facilities covered under the small craft harbours legislation. Of these, approximately 1,500 are used for fishing and some 800 for recreation. From the figures we can readily see the number of people who are affected by this legislation, yet the minister gave no indication either in his remarks this morning nor in the bill as to the government's intentions with regard to increased sums of money to be made available for needed improvement of the many facilities which this bill places under his care.
December 10, 1976

If we look at the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1977, we find that the total budgetary amount for the fisheries and marine program under the heading of "Environment" comes to $261,016,000. There are many comparisons that can be made with that figure and the amounts allocated to other government departments: namely, the CBC, $416 million; Atomic Energy of Canada, a department which we are hearing quite a bit about these days, $97 million; the National Capital Commission, $53 million; the National Arts Centre, $8 million. We spent something like $50 million on erecting the building, and now it cannot operate without a subsidy of $8 million just so people can see the show.
The CBC will receive from the public purse in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1977, a hand-out of $416 million. This amount is in addition to any they may take in from any other source through the sale of advertising. The payola works out to $8 million a week for programs whose content is very seriously questioned by my constituents on an almost monthly basis. The CBC receives more than one and one half times the amount of money allocated by this government for its fisheries and marine program on both coasts and in central Canada. In my opinion, this is too low a priority rating when one considers the vast areas of Canada covered by the fishing industry and the large number of men, women and children who are entirely dependent upon this primary industry for their very survival.
I believe the minister is working hard. He is making an honest effort. He is trying. I believe he is hoping for a better future for our fishermen. I give him credit for that. However, many of the people in the area covered by this legislation have survived for many years on hope. But that hope, I say to the minister sincerely, is now turning to despair. At the present time, on the Atlantic coast there are approximately 39,000 fishermen of whom only about 3,000 are on the offshore fleet. The rest are all inshore fishermen, dependent on small craft harbours as a base for landing their craft. They hope to have security for their ships and fishing equipment when high winds and heavy seas force them from the fishing banks.
Under this bill, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) is given a sacred trust. He is being given a responsibility to ensure that adequate facilities will be provided for the safety, lives and equipment of some 36,000 inshore fishermen in Atlantic Canada alone. Since fishing markets are mostly external to Canada, it is essential, indeed, vital that this nation keep its fishing industry as efficient as any in the world. Up to this point I have been speaking only of the inshore fleet. However, our offshore fleet also requires consideration by this government.
At the present time, some 12 companies, owning approximately 50 plants, of which some 25 are served by the offshore fleet, account for approximately 80 per cent of Canada's fresh and frozen groundfish production and about 45 per cent of the total fishing production of Atlantic Canada. This fleet is struggling today. The captains are struggling to find the large volumes of raw materials required for 12 months of operation on a mass production basis. What does this bill do for them? If they increase their costs, it will knock Canada out of the
Fishing and Recreational Harbours highly competitive world markets it presently enjoys as a seafood supplier. Both our inshore and offshore fleets are vitally important to the Canadian economy. However, I say to this House that our only chance to exploit the fisheries resources to the extremities of our 200-mile zone and beyond this area is with a modern, efficient fleet working on a 12-month basis.
We have the expertise; we have the know-how in Atlantic Canada. We need only a management team interested in the recovery and harvesting control of our resource to give Atlantic Canada a restored and thriving fishing industry. As the resource recovered, we could triple our present volume without adding appreciably to the number of ships in operation today, thereby assuring steady employment for our Fishermen and plant workers.
Here I must mention a very important adjunct to the fishing industry, our plant workers. Shore plant workers in our east coast fishing plants are facing economic hardship today due to the mismanagement of our fisheries resources by this government over the past ten years. Recently, a weekly newspaper printed a cheque stub from the pay cheque of an average wage earner in an east coast plant. The cheque stub showed 34.25 hours worked at regular time, $3.90 per hour, and 12 hours of Saturday overtime at $5.85 per hour. The gross earnings were $207.53, while the net earnings were $171.43. Even you, Mr. Speaker, might say that is not bad for a week's work. However, you would be,adopting the wrong premise because the figures I have just quoted cover a two-week work period. It works out to $85.71 per week. Out of this amount, he or she has to pay the rent, or mortgage, food, fuel oil, clothing, electricity, operate a car to and from work, plus gas and all the rest of a family's expenses. This, I say, is about average for plant workers as a whole.
When there are no fish to process, the work force is sent home as the employees are paid only for the hours worked. The Anti-Inflation Board obviously did not take that factor into consideration when it made decisions about wage levels. The Minister of Fisheries and his officials obviously did not take it into consideration when they established fisheries quotas for 1976 and 1977, quotas which force the fisherman to limit his fishing activities, quotas which force him to spead out his fishing effort over a longer term. This action will in the long run spread out the economic and social hardship for shore workers over a longer period.
Only this week I asked the Minister of Fisheries a question in the House about discussions he was having with the industry concerning quotas. He replied that he was hopeful that he could spread the quotas for the next year over a 12-month period. That, I know, was not an intentional statement by the minister. It could not have been. It shows a gross lack of knowledge of what happens when you encourage men who want to go to sea, men who want to work to the best of their capability to catch the biggest catch available to them, telling them to spread out their capability, spreading out the Fishing quotas so that they will only land smaller quotas per trip. Think of what this is doing to the shore plant worker. I just

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours gave a classic example of what is happening at present and has been happening throughout 1976, yet next year they are not promised more of the same, but even a little less of the same. The minister is, in effect, saying that $85.71 a week is enough for a shore worker. Surely we can do better than that.
We are establishing a 200-mile limit, hopefully for the benefit of Canadians and not entirely for the benefit of foreign nationals. Hopefully, it will be for the benefit of shore plant workers in Atlantic Canada. However, this is the ultimate result of the minister's action when he says we will spread out quotas. He is simply spreading out inefficiency. It is not encouraging initiative. It does not encourage people who are ambitious and want to work. This is making it more difficult for our people, both ashore and afloat, to earn an honest living. The fishing industry of Canada obviously requires a higher profile. It needs a spending priority equal to or higher than that of the CBC, since the fishing industry directly and indirectly affects the livelihood of so many Canadians. Unfortunately, Bill C-7 gives little or no recognition to the validity of many of the points I have raised. It does, however, grant the minister wide powers. Clauses 5(1) reads as follows:
The minister may undertake projects for the acquisition, development, con-truction, improvement or repair of any scheduled harbour or any fishing or recreational harbour to which this act applies.
Clause 8 provides:
The minister may, subject to the regulations,
(a)	lease any scheduled harbour or any part thereof to any person,
(b)	grant a licence to any person for the use of any scheduled harbour or any
part thereof, and
(c)	enter into any agreement with the government of any province or any
agency thereof for the occupancy or use of any scheduled harbour or any part
thereof.
Knowing the character of the minister, and knowing the character of various members on this side of the House-one of whom, I believe, will be the minister of fisheries after the 1978 election-I am sure these wide powers will not be abused. However, this does not mean they should remain on the books. I was always of the opinion, for example, that our harbours belonged to the public. I cannot understand how any minister could believe he had the right to lease harbours or any part of a harbour to one person. Surely, limits should be set on the application of clause 8 when the measure is sent to committee.
Under this bill, the minister can build recreational harbours wherever he chooses, without regard for provincial or municipal desires. What has happened to the view that the provinces should be consulted on matters which affect their interests? I say to the minister most sincerely that lack of consultation over fisheries matters with provincial ministers is a major criticism of him, and that it is advanced not only by Conservative provincial ministers but by Liberal provincial ministers as well. The government is becoming increasingly involved in the building of recreational harbours. It has taken the path of shared-cost programs with the provinces; it pays up to 50 per cent of the cost, but only for breakwaters and dredging.

Provincial and municipal governments pay the other costs, as well as the cost of annual upkeep.
Unfortunately, the number of recreational harbours is increasing while the number of government fishing wharves is decreasing. I am not opposed to recreational harbours being established, since they are beneficial to the tourist industry, to visiting yachtsmen when they come to Canada from the United States or other countries. However, I submit they should not be built at the expense of our fishermen or of our fishing industry which is presently being denied adequate facilities in many parts of Canada. In my own town of Lunenburg, for example, there is a desperate need for further docking space for our scallop fleet. In Vogler's Cove, Nova Scotia, the inshore fleet requires another 60 feet added to the present wharf in order that the longliners may have adequate protection. In the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of October 30, we read, under the heading "Smithville fishermen still waiting for wharf', the following report from Shelburne county:
Four years after being promised a new wharf by the federal government to replace the existing decrepit structure which is the focal point of fisheries activities in this small Atlantic coast port, Fishermen are still forced to operate from the same primitive facility which has been in existence for many years.
"Any good storm or even a high tide could easily wash this wharf out tomorrow and then where would the fishermen tie up?" asks Kendrick Sears, a veteran fisherman and operator of a small handling plant by the wharf. "Conditions here are unbelievable. Several years ago one section of the docking facilities completely collapsed under the weight of a hundred lobster traps. Although recovered by their owners, the traps were damaged beyond all recognition." Mr. Sears says instances like this have not been uncommon and as a result fishermen in the area were notified five years ago that a new wharf was on its way.
I did not check, but that must have been an election year. The report continues:
"Our wharf was supposed to be constructed immediately after the wharf at Shag Harbour, Shelburne county", he said. "It's been four years since then and we still have no decent facilities."
I hope the minister will put that one in his little black book when he starts in on his new duties. Last week I was privileged to visit Newfoundland. The Newfoundland members are quite capable of calling attention to the lack of facilities in their province and laying deficiencies at the door of the minister. But I hear, from discussions with the fishermen, that they have been waiting for ten years for a slipway and wharf at Wild Cove, White Bay; they have been waiting at Nipper's Harbour for a comparable period of time without either hauling facilities or landing facilities.
My hon. friends from other provinces intend to speak today. They will deal with their own areas, so I shall deal only with the figures provided to me as they relate to Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia-and these figures were provided to me by the government-how do we fare on the list of expenditures by provinces in connection with the harbour development program? In 1973-74 we received $1,607,181. The year 1974-75 was an election year; we received $5,814,000. In 1975-76 we received $4,625,400. That is little more than half the sum the government made available to keep the National Arts Centre show going just down the street. If you want to see Liberace there, you only pay $6 or $7 because the people in Nova
December 10, 1976

Scotia, the people in Atlantic Canada help pay a subsidy to keep the show going in a place they never even see. They never even see the building, still less do they have an occasion to see a show there.

speechtext: The mandarins see it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
That is correct. It is a national disgrace that we should be held in such contempt by the government of Canada because this is the smallest amount they can conceivably give us. It is unreal when one reads reports as to the effects of this type of policy. I could give many more examples, but it seems to me that the Department of Fisheries, which is now responsible for small craft harbour development, hopes to abandon or destroy obsolete wharves and, instead, arrange that a whole area is served by one central government facility.
Since government wharves are essential to the livelihood of many of our small fishing communities-and this is true whether one is considering the coastal areas of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec or British Columbia-I ask the minister this question: Does he have a master plan for the future of small craft harbours? If so, it would be most helpful if he laid his cards on the table so that this plan could be discussed when the bill before us goes to committee.
At the same time, since it would appear that the government is becoming increasingly involved with recreational harbours, it would be interesting to know the extent to which it proposes to stretch its powers in this field. How far, for example, does the government propose to go in carrying out its marina assistance program which was established to encourage the construction of marinas by local municipalities and private developers? The federal government pays for the construction of a breakwater and for dredging, while the municipality or the developer, sometimes both, pay the other costs plus upkeep. The government pays 50 per cent of the cost, yet despite this receives no compensation in return for its contribution.
Many fishermen are asking why the government should spend the taxpayers' money in this manner. Is the department at least taking steps to ensure that these marinas will be open and available to all boats, at reasonable cost? I have a further question for the minister. If the yachtsmen pay nothing to the government for the use of marinas, by what yardstick should fishermen be taxed when they tie up their boats to a government wharf? I should like that explained in detail, Mr. Speaker, either here or in committee.
This bill gives the government power to make regulations for the control of mooring, berthing, loading or discharging of vessels, for controlling pollution, for prescribing standards for the accommodation and services provided, for prescribing charges for the use of any scheduled harbour, for prescribing the duties of persons appointed to supervise or manage any fishing or recreational harbour to which the act applies, and for prescribing the remuneration to be paid to officers or
Fishing and Recreational Harbours employees appointed to carry out the provisions of the act. Those powers, under the regulations in this bill, can only mean one thing, Mr. Speaker; namely, more civil servants, more inspectors and still more expenses loaded on to the backs of Canadian fishermen-and all of this, I submit, at a time when their burdens were never greater, when their fisheries resources were never smaller, having been raped, pillaged and plundered by foreign nationals.
These are new charges by this government in an area where 14 per cent or more of our people are unemployed. It is an area already suffering under the burden of unfair and unjust transportation charges, an area, I submit, in which energy costs are higher than in any other area of Canada. This type of thinking, Mr. Speaker, this type of legislation, represents the lack of concern shown by this government for the needs of our people.
It seems to me that this bill can only be classed as an extension of the user-pay concept proposed to our people by the Minister of Transport, a concept which will bring ruination to our farmers, our fishermen and to many of our industries in Atlantic Canada. It is a concept that is not enforced on the users of our airports, or the St. Lawrence Seaway, the cost of which already is in excess of $800 million. It does not apply to the CBC. Why does the government subsidize Mirabel, for example, to the tune of $46 million for one year's operations? That is $16 million more than the government is going to give to all of Atlantic Canada, to all of central Canada and to all of western Canada for harbour development. It is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker.
Why single out our fishermen and require them to bear such an unfair burden? We in Atlantic Canada have to look at this legislation in the light of what the government is doing to our people, and this is the way it comes out at our end. Call us what you will. Say that we are looking at this from the wrong end of the telescope, if you like; but that is the way we see it, Mr. Speaker. It is away past the time that this government woke up and did something concrete and in a responsible manner for the people in our area along the lines that I have been suggesting.
I realize that at the present time there are wharfage charges on the books which were determined in the 1880s and they are clearly out of date today. There are men who are supposed to collect wharfage fees, but since this is a low paying job not every government facility is manned and this collection is not being made. This has resulted in a situation where most fishermen have paid no fees. However, under Bill C-7 the government plans to appoint zone managers and they will look after a general area. They will have broad powers of enforcement, with the right to board any vessel and seize, detain or sell any ship whose owner does not comply fully with these regulations. I submit that if there is one thing that the fishing industry does not need at the present time, it is a whole new army of inspectors and officers who will have the right to fine a fisherman for any infraction of these new rules. There will be a minimum fine of $50. It may not sound like much to a bureaucrat in Ottawa, but sometimes $50 is very difficult to come by if you are a fisherman in Atlantic Canada.

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
In addition, Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that the minister plans a special treat for our fishermen. Instead of having people collect daily wharfage fees, an annual licence will be required, I understand. The figure that I heard discussed is $1 per foot per fishing vessel per year. This licence will allow the fishermen to use any government wharf at any time. However, in my view this is simply another unfair tax on Canadians using public facilities in Atlantic Canada, while people in more prosperous areas of our nation are provided public facilities free of charge.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that we would support the bill because there should be consolidation, in our opinion, in one act for all the policies and programs that now exist. The authority of the minister over small craft harbours, which he has had since 1973, has only been derived from a letter or warrant from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This bill at least gives him the proper authority to carry out his duties in the area of small craft harbours. However, that does not mean that we on this side totally agree with the wide powers that are being granted to the minister. We want to see changes made in the bill, changes which will make this legislation more acceptable to our Canadian fishermen and recognize their valid needs without placing unjust charges upon them or their families.

Mr. Speaker, I have had a brief opportunity to review the bill presently under discussion. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), I believe, described this as a housekeeping bill. It does not do anything particularly significant in terms of assisting those who are in the most difficult position of trying to make a living from our oceans. It is interesting to note that there has not really been any change in government policy or in the way it assesses transportation needs in Canada or how we should go about satisfying them. What the bill says, in effect, is that we are going to promote recreational harbours on some kind of an agreed formula at some other time, and at some indefinite point in the future we might come to some agreement in terms of providing additional fishing harbours.
This is exactly the kind of pig-in-a-poke we have been getting ever since I came to this place in 1972. The people, specifically fishermen, want to know how much the federal government is going to pay for these fishing harbours. We have received this kind of promise and suggestion in the past,
[Mr. Crouse.J
especially before an election when our friends in the cabinet travel to various small ports in British Columbia saying, "Here is another little place where we are going to have a dock, and for all you fellows who are having trouble on the other side of the bay, we are going to look after it."

speechtext: We will build the breakwaters.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: It is like the annual promise. I hope the people of British Columbia will not be fooled by this little piece of housekeeping legislation. There is no significant change in this government's failure to provide meaningful tie-up facilities for small boats in British Columbia. The reason there is no change is, quite frankly, that this government does not understand anything about water transportation in B.C. If you go out to B.C. and you go to a small place such as Pender Harbour-

speechtext: -you fellows from Ontario definitely need some instruction on the needs of water transportation in B.C. I would like to take my good friend out to a place called Pender Harbour. You cannot get from one point to another in B.C., in some places, without taking a boat. Yes. He will have to get down to Toronto on a subsidized road. Then we go from Toronto to Vancouver on a subsidized aircraft and land at a subsidized airport where the people of B.C. continue to funnel money for those kinds of transportation. But the man who is running the little boat in B.C. whom you are going to visit is getting darned little in terms of his transportation needs. Who will pay for getting this man from one small port to another? Not only is he getting darned little, but the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has even taken away the little bit he used to get, which was a subsidy of about $4 million-peanuts for this government. The government is ideologically locked into a philosophy which will not work in transportation.
I might say that my friends to the right are operating under exactly the same kind of delusion, namely, that you can run a transportation system in Canada on the basis of the user-pay concept. We have never done it yet, and we never will. If this government wants to talk about user-pay, it should have started with the CPR when that railway spanned this country with a piece of rail. We gave them massive amounts of wealth for that. Now we are talking about user-pay. Why does the government not start asking CPR to give back some of the
December 10,1976

millions of acres and tremendous resources that the people of Canada gave them in order to put that ribbon of steel across the country? Only then should we start talking about the user-pay concept.

speechtext: Plus all the cash grants.

If you fly over it, you realize it is still a string of settlements and we are trying to connect the people together. The user-pay concept means one thing; it means that the rich will fly and the poor will walk. It means that the poor people who live in villages in B.C. in the isolated north will suddenly find the cost of everything they buy and everything they ship out has gone up. Let me tell you that if you live in Ocean Falls, as the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall) knows very well, and you do not see a major vessel come into that port, it is not a very good place to be. I know; I used to work on the coast. It is not a good place to be only because the government does not understand the necessity of holding down the cost of living in those communities for people to live there and to enjoy it. I want to get back to the bill, because if you live in a small community surrounded by water and you expect this bill to help you, you should know what the facts are.
First, you do not know how much the federal government is going to pay. The first thing you will need is dredging; then you will need a breakwater if you live, for example, in the Gulf Islands. In most cases you need a breakwater because the wash takes away most of the docks. Fifty per cent of that cost, if you can get approval, will be borne by the government. Most of these breakwaters cost $3 million or $4 million. Are you asking the local residents to pick up the difference? Don't be ridiculous. There is no way you can ask those people, who quite often are on low incomes and quite often struggle to make a living from the ocean or from the forest, to find that kind of money.
But then you think about what we have spent at Mirabel airport for members of the House of Commons to fly around, and for others. When you think of what we are proposing to spend at Vancouver international airport for a third runway, $500 million for people like me and the rest of us, you realize that perhaps we should think about the people who do not fly all the time because, believe it or not, only about 10 per cent of
Fishing and Recreational Harbours the Canadian public flies on any kind of regular basis. The rest of the people are struggling with other forms of transport which are being frozen out, denuded.
What is happening is that alternate forms of transport, such as rail and water transportation, are being wiped out because of lack of attention by this government and, to some extent, by the provincial government. In order to understand the current emergency in B.C., one has to look briefly at the history. Somehow or other everybody seems to think that this happened suddenly in November when the minister decided to end the subsidy to Northland Navigation. Some of us who have worked on this since last July have written letters to the minister. We warned him about what would happen, and so did trade unions, businesses and chambers of commerce. It is not as though this government did not know. They had every opportunity to admit they had a problem and that they knew this policy would not work. They could have said, "Let us go out to the coast and find out what has happened". What are they doing now? They are going there after the mess has been created, after they find out the major shipping company there, Northland Navigation, may not be interested in coming back because they have lost all their employees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be fair to say that fisheries in general has tended to be a low profile ministry. I do not think it has been low profile just in the last few years, however, but since confederation fisheries has not been one of the "gutsy" departments that has caused a great deal of soul-searching in Canada or has gripped the imagination of central Canada. Perhaps that is a shame. I think the fact that the two extremities of the country, the maritimes and British Columbia, are the regions most concerned may explain why it has not been a high profile ministry. I can only congratulate the minister because I think we are becoming a little higher in profile.
Should we have a low profile when 77,000 people are employed in the fisheries of Canada? Should we have a low profile when approximately $700 million is accruing from commercial fisheries, and out of that $400 million goes directly into exports to help our balance of payments? I wonder if we should continue to have a low profile when there are over
800.000	pleasure craft in Canada and 70,000 visiting tourist craft? Are we talking about something that should continue to have a low profile? The minister has indicated there are approximately 2,300 harbours under his jurisdiction and
38.000	fishing vessels in Canada on both coasts. Is it perhaps time for the low profile to be discarded and for the people of Canada-not just of the maritimes and British Columbia-to become a little more interested in what is happening in those two areas with respect to transportation and fisheries?
I think the profile has been raised, if for no other reason than we took one of the most momentous decisions in our history when we declared, in Bill C-177, that we would extend our jurisdiction to 200 miles off the Pacific and Atlantic coastlines and in March will extend it to 200 miles in the Arctic. I think many people, whether they be in Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, are beginning to realize the untapped wealth of our coastlines and how it will not only benefit British Columbia and the maritimes but all Canadians. The question of the 200-mile economic zone has focused the attention of Canadians on an area where there was not much interest before. I trust this will give a much higher profile to the minister and his department, a profile that I think they deserve.
As a result of negotiations carried on by the federal government and the distant water fishing nations, a treaty has been signed between 90 per cent of those nations and Canada. This will enable Canada, not to go into a 200-mile cod war or any other kind of war but to go in with signed agreements. I am sure our United States friends wish they were in Canada's enviable position, because this government has done an excellent job in laying the groundwork for the 200-mile economic zone.

I presume he was referring to electrical and water services. May I point out that the provision of wharf facilities costs this government a great deal of money. If a fee were not charged, it would mean that some users would get a much better deal than others. We should not do as the hon. member suggests. Instead, I suggest that we should approach this matter as we approach the licensing of motor vehicles. I submit that once you have paid your annual fee, you should be entitled to tie up at any federal wharf or port.
I hope the minister will introduce that system, which would be fair. This system should be run in the way motor vehicle licensing is run. For example, in certain outlying parts of British Columbia motorists are forced to drive on unpaved roads or gravelled roads. But all motorists, no matter what kind of roads they drive on, are forced to pay a licence fee for the motor vehicle. Part of the licence fee will be used, hopefully, to improve road facilities. Similarly, I hope a standard system of collecting wharf fees will be introduced. At the present time it is eminently unfair to charge some and ten miles away charge others. We should have a user fee on a yearly basis. Those people should use government facilities on an equal basis. I trust that those fees will then be turned back into small craft harbours to improve and upgrade the present facilities. I hope that is the system.
I hope I have answered the hon. member's question, because I think it is a very important part of this legislation. In the two and one half years I have sat on the fisheries committee, I have asked for that sort of system. I think we are now getting it. Therefore, that is an improvement.

The small craft harbours, law of the sea, and salmon enhancement are all part of what I call the infrastructure which provides a system of national management of the oceans' resources. I take the sea salmon as one part of this infrastructure. It is a great pleasure to have that sort of rational management going forward with all these items being brought together. It is nice to have jurisdiction over the

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours 200-mile limit, but you need other things in place. I was pleased with the announcement that search and rescue facilities on both the east and west coasts will be increased. This is, again, putting it together because they are all related.
I was pleased with the announcement by the minister that Bill C-7 would go ahead. I realize that on the east coast of Canada there are some problems in so far as concerns charging fees at certain government installations. In British Columbia we have a system whereby commercial fishermen as well as sports fishermen pay for the use of government facilities. The problem there is that some have paid and some have not. I suggest we should have a system whereby fishermen and people in the recreational boating field are treated equally. Rather than some paying and others not, all should have the same responsibility. After all, they are all users of the system. If you are going to use the facility, you have some responsibility toward contributing to its upkeep as well as making a contribution toward upgrading the facilities. I hope the hon. member for New Westminster will agree with that.
The upgrading and creation of new wharf facilities, new rafts and new boat docking facilities is something that members of all parties would like to see. There may be some question as to implementation, and that is a valid point. However, all members should realize that this bill is an attempt to improve upon something that has existed for many years, but it has not given the minister a cohesive or rational method for planning. Recreational boaters will be pleased that community, municipal and provincial governments will be allowed some flexibility with regard to promoting recreational boating on the east and west coasts as well as Ontario.

That would distort the system. In that I agree with the minister.
On that point, I would first urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to undertake a joint federal-provincial study of transportation on the west coast of British Columbia, including not only water but air and, in specific cases, both rail and land. Second, I urge the minister to hold public hearings in the affected areas and also other areas where there is an interest in this problem. Third, I urge the minister to involve members of parliament from all parties in this study. I believe it is important that members of this House take an active role in an area of transportation which affects the livelihood, both social and economic, of those on the west coast of Canada.
The minister should implement the recommendations of such a study as soon as possible. Members of all parties should look in a non-partisan way at how we can improve transportation on the west coast of Canada. speechtext:
This bill proposes a system of zone managers. I would like to ask the minister whether this is going to be a refuge for old Liberal poll captains and the like. Is this another opening for patronage? When the minister answers I want him to inform the House whether the zone managers who look after public harbours are going to be appointed through the Public Service Commission on the merit system, or are they going to be another example of the patronage system in Atlantic and Pacific Canada, the patronage system that was referred to by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). Are we going to have zone managers whose only qualification is that they are ex-Liberal supporters? The government will not find an active Liberal in Newfoundland so it would have to be an ex-supporter, and even then the government will have a job to find one. I should like to know whether the zone managers are going to be political appointments or public service appointments.
Let me warn the hon. gentleman that if he tries to impose a system for collecting fees for small craft using harbours in Newfoundland and the poor fisherman comes in with his 25 foot or 30 foot vessel, and the minister is going to ask him for $20 to tie up his boat, then he is going to be in severe difficulties.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: He had better watch out for harpoons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Yes, he will have to watch out for harpoons, because our fishermen are not used to having to pay anything to tie up their boats at public wharves. The wharves and their facilities will have to be simply magnificent if the minister is to

persuade them to pay something out of their meagre earnings for a licensing system. I suggest to the minister that on political grounds, if for no other reason, he will have to tread pretty carefully in this regard. I believe that in theory everyone should pay for public facilities that are provided to them, but that is not the way it has been in the past in Newfoundland, and it will be a pretty difficult system to institute.
I believe that the Minister of Transport's user-pay principle is like a disease which seems to be spreading to other ministers. I suggest to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment that he take an inoculation so that he will not catch the user-pay disease of the Minister of Transport.
There are a number of places in the constituency of St. John's West where wharves and harbours do need some improvement now. I will not list every one of them, but there is Tors Cove, Point Lance where they have just suffered tremendous damage from a wind storm three or four weeks ago and the wharf facility and community stage were pretty well destroyed, St. Bride's, Southern Harbour, and several other places in the district. I hope that the minister will tell the House that some of the $1.7 million will be used in these areas to help repair the damage that has been suffered.
I would also like the hon. gentleman to keep in mind that a fishing operation is still being conducted from the port of St. John's. There are some 40 to 50 fishermen who fish from St. John's and the facilities they use for tying up their boats are very poor. There is no room for them to haul them out of the water. Although St. John's is not a small harbour, the facilities there for the fishermen are very inadequate. If the minister would see whether he could help out in this regard with the port authorities, it would be much appreciated and would fit within the scope of this legislation. I ask him not to forget the city of St. John's just because it is a large urban area.

speechtext: He did not forget Port aux Basques.

I am glad the hon. member mentioned that because it is a sore point with me. You cannot get to a port or a harbour, Mr. Speaker, unless you can safely navigate your way there. A problem has been caused in Placentia Bay because of the downgrading of the traffic control system for vessels using Placentia Bay. I should just like to give some figures to the minister. On the east side of Placentia Bay there are 56 long liners. The west side of Placentia Bay is in the constituency of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson); the east side is in my district.
These 56 long liners have to cross the tracks that are set for tankers and other vessels moving up and down Placentia Bay in order to get to their fishing grounds. In addition to these 56 long liners, a 1972 inventory showed that from St. Bride's to Woody Island there were 284 motorboats and 1,136 rowboats, small boats which are used for fishing. Placentia Bay is known to be a bay which often has fog.
There was a vessel traffic control system established there with headquarters in Argentia, which had particular connections with the opening of the oil refinery at Come-by-Chance. When the oil refinery suspended operation last February, the
December 10, 1976

Minister of Transport and his minions in Newfoundland lost no time dismantling this traffic control centre in Placentia Bay. Presumably they have no faith in the oil refinery reopening. In the last couple of days of the election campaign, I discovered on October 16 that these scoundrels were dismantling the radar facilities at Cuslett in Placentia Bay.

speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Do you know what they were doing with them, Mr. Speaker? They were taking them to Port aux Basques, which is in the constituency of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The people of St. John's West showed what they thought about that; the Liberal candidate got 16 per cent of the vote, and that was a miracle. They biodegraded-a good bureaucratic word-the radar facilities at Cuslett and moved them to Port aux Basques for a traffic control system there. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what kind of government is that?
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but as I have said a memorandum was sent round to the coast guard telling them that the candidate for the P.C. party had raised this issue publicly, that he had asked for a public inquiry, and that they were not to say a word to anyone. Everything was to be referred to the head of the coast guard in Newfoundland. I am not going to forget that, Mr. Speaker. I have asked the minister questions about it in the House, I have written two letters to him about it, but I still have received no answer from him. What kind of traffic control system is there now at Placentia Bay so that we can know that our 284 motorboats, our 1,136 rowboats and our 56 long liners, the CN coastal boats, the phosphorous ships that go back and forth along the harbour carrying a most dangerous cargo-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: And the minister's yacht.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
-and the minister's yacht which docks at Sound Island, are safe? The minister has a summer place now at Sound Island, appropriately named. He is in danger too. What kind of a traffic control system do we now have in Placentia Bay? Is it safe, and is navigation safe? I did not want to bring this matter up in the House because I thought I might irritate the hon. gentleman who is Secretary of State for External Affairs, but it is safe for me to do it today because I understand he is in Europe and he may not notice my comments in Hansard. I do not want to incur the hon. gentleman's wrath but I will be reminding him about this matter in the future.
How are the fishermen going to get back and forth to their ports and harbours in Placentia Bay safely? If the Minister of Transport will not give me the answer, I would like to ask the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment to satisfy himself that the downgraded, cannibalized traffic system in Placentia Bay is still adequate to protect the fishermen of Placentia Bay. I would like the minister's assurance that he is satisfied that it is so, because I am having difficulty getting any assurance from the Minister of Transport.

speechtext:
There are a number of ports on the south coast opposite the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, which for the information of the House are two French islands. We are rather puzzled about what is happening to St. Pierre and Miquelon and the fishing harbours that lie across from St. Pierre and Miquelon. Is the issue settled or not settled? Does the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment realize the danger that, if St. Pierre and Miquelon declare a 200-mile limit, the district of Burin-Burgeo will disappear and with it the Secretary of State for External Affairs? I admit that this could be a blessing in disguise, Mr. Speaker, but what is the position in regard to St. Pierre and Miquelon?
Where is the boundary line between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and the coast of Newfoundland, and what is being proposed as the fisheries arrangement between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Newfoundland? I will not pursue that further because I know I may be straying a bit from the main principle of this bill. I would ask the Minister if he could deal with that as it would be of help. When he replies perhaps he would also deal with the traffic system.
Soon we will not have any inshore fisheries in Newfoundland. This will have gone the same way as the animals which have now disappeared; the same way as the whooping crane, the American buffalo, and the Canadian Liberal. They will all have vanished if the hon. gentleman opposite does not do something to preserve our inshore fisheries. If the fish do not come inshore the inshore fishermen cannot catch fish. That would appear to me to be something that does not require very much elucidation. This puzzles me, and perhaps the minister can deal with this too when he answers.
What puzzles me is what consideration is given to the inshore fishermen when the quotas are set at ICNAF for various specimens of fish. Fish can only come inshore if they are not caught offshore. My concern relates to the subject of a question I asked today about redfish. That is a species caught mostly for the plants on the south coast of Newfoundland. It is difficult to understand what has happened in respect of quotas for redfish.
As the minister knows, the Canadian quota for redfish was used up by September of this year. That left three months when these plants in the Burin-Burgeo area, also the area of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, had no supply. This also affected several other plants on the south coast. The boats could no longer go out and fish for the redfish. Their gear and vessels are not suited for fishing for other species, although they are now attempting that. Since the end of September these plants have been operating one or two days a week. The plant workers only have one or two days' work each week. The owners are losing money when their vessels only get

I am glad to hear that, Mr. Speaker. If I have the position correctly, there has been no decision made regarding a special program as yet, but the minister will be carrying on a review every three months. What puzzles me is that this year, 1976, the quota accepted by Canada for redfish was 43,300 tons, while for other nations fishing in this area 200 miles offshore the quota was 76,700 tons out of a total catch of
120.000	tons. Those were the figures for redfish for 1976 in ICNAF sub-areas, 2, 3 and 4. For 1977 Canada has apparently agreed that our quota will be 62,950 tons out of a total of
116.000	tons. This is certainly an improvement, but there will still be 53,000 tons allowed for other nations in sub-areas 2, 3 and 4. I would ask how we can contemplate allowing these foreign countries to catch even that much redfish in view of our experience this year when plants had to close because they used up their quota of redfish in nine months?
When the minister replies and deals with the general situation, I would like him to deal with what puzzles me in respect of inshore fisheries. Are the inshore fishermen taken into consideration in these computations and when the quotas are decided upon? If the fish do not come in for them to catch we do not need any small craft harbours, and we will not need the expenditure of these moneys. We are not being asked to vote the money now, but we will certainly not need this kind of a structure. We will not need the money if there is no inshore fishery.
There is a clause in the bill that gives the minister the right to lease facilities. I do not know whether the legislation requires this, but the minister will be empowered, if he wishes, to lease what I presume are wharves and other facilities. I personally feel it would be a very good idea if the legislation required the minister to table copies of any leases that are entered into for facilities. These leases should be filed here in the House. We should not have to ask about them, this should be automatic. If the minister leases any facility, a copy of the lease should be tabled automatically in the House of Commons. When the bill goes to the committee I will be asking about this and I would like the minister to consider it. The bill does not now provide for it, as far as I know.
There are a number of other matters I could touch on and address in respect of this bill, but there are other members who are anxious to speak this afternoon, so let me just reiterate.
One of the danger areas here, and I suggest the minister is going to have some difficulty, is in a licencing system which
involves the payment of fees by inshore fishermen who do not average a very high income per year, as the minister knows. This is going to be one area of danger.
I would also like to touch on the question of whether this bill indicates greater attention in respect of small craft harbours, and I would ask whether the minister is going to institute a program involving icemaking facilities which can be used in connection with these small harbours and the community stage program? Will the minister also let us know at what stage the community stage program for Newfoundland is at this time? Does he think that next year he will be able to go ahead with the agreement to turn over the federal community stages to the province once they are put into proper repair, or once proper repairs have been done?
There are some LIP projects being carried out with the assistance of the small craft and harbours branch. This is making it possible for a number of small jobs in local communities to be carried out, both in St. John's West and other areas of Newfoundland. These LIP projects could not be carried out without the help of the department in obtaining the materials required. In practice this is a good program because this small craft and harbours branch makes sure the projects are sensible and keeps an eye on them to see that they are carried out properly. The only thing is, of course, that we should not leave it to LIP projects to provide for the building and repairing of wharves, breakwaters, and other facilities of that nature. Really the government should be doing this. However, in the circumstances there is not a sufficient amount of money being voted. I would like to express my thanks to the minister and the small craft and harbours branch for the facilities they are providing in Newfoundland. Many of these facilities would not have been provided without the LIP program and without the assistance of this branch.
I will end my comments at this stage by saying that this bill is going to establish a much better administration structure for small craft harbours. I am glad to see it is in the hands of the Minister of Fisheries. He is a man who will be interested in seeing that the moneys are properly used. I hope we will see more money voted in respect of small craft harbours next year when the estimates come before us, as well as more money for public works expenditures in Newfoundland generally, where our unemployment rate is ferocious, being in excess of 14 per cent; actually much higher because of our low participation rate. These are the kinds of projects we need to get us over this difficult period.
I congratulate the minister on his bill. The only thing I worry about is whether the rest of his colleagues will give him the financial means to carry out the job properly. I congratulate the minister on his actions. He is a highly regarded Minister of Fisheries. It is too bad we cannot say the same thing for some of his colleagues, and it is too bad that fisheries does not get more attention from the Government of Canada.
