speechtext:
It is important to see this bill in context. I do not want to make lengthy remarks on it, but I think it is important to note some points.
It is important to see this bill in the context of what is happening in fisheries, and indeed in the context of the 200 mile limit. That limit is important. It is important to control foreign Fishing, to be able to tell foreign fishing fleets where they can fish and how much they can Fish. Also we should be able to control our own fishing because we have to provide for the replenishment of stocks. The Hamilton Bank is not far from the coast of my own riding, and I and my fishermen are well aware of the importance of that area as a spawning ground, as is indeed the whole of the northeastern shore of that coast. It is important to have that 200 mile limit and to be able to control our quotas so as to allow our stocks to build up again.
But we must realize the inherent conflict between the offshore and inshore fisheries. That is true whether foreign fleets fish off our shores or indeed whether Canadian fleets do so. I think this bill is an indication of faith in the inshore fisheries. The hon. member for St. John's West mentioned in his speech the necessity for building up those stocks, the necessity for

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours setting quotas to allow for the prosecution of inshore fisheries. I want to make that point and make it as soundly as I possibly can.
There will of course be an offshore fleet-nobody will turn off the machine. The machine is with us and is going to be used. The offshore fleet is there and supposedly it is going to grow, but it is going to grow according to our regulations and policies, and according to our say-so. But there is conflict between the offshore and inshore fisheries, and in setting the quotas we must provide the necessary protection for inshore fishermen. There must be some fish left to escape inshore because there will certainly be an inshore fishery along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador for some time to come. We must protect our fishermen and we must support them, and I see this bill as an indication of support for them.
Joint ventures have been mentioned, particularly by the government of which the hon. member for St. John's West was formerly a member. I do not know what the specific plans are for joint ventures. We have not heard them enunciated in detail, but I think we should look at them with some caution. I think we must have a Canada first policy with regard to our catching capability, and our efforts should be directed to building up our own fleet. If there are to be any joint ventures, they must of necessity be very short-term and for very specific reasons and in specific areas, with proper safeguards built in for the build up of the Canadian fishing industry. This is one of those plans enunciated by the provincial government in Newfoundland which we have not seen come fully to fruition. The $40 million plan for trawlers was another one we did not see come to fruition, but if it comes to life and we know what the details will be, we will have to look at it with some caution because 1 think it will be important for the Canadian industry and, as I said before, important for inshore fishermen.
The small craft harbours branch in our province is doing a fantastic job, in my view. The hon. member for St. John's West has already mentioned some of the points I was going to make with regard to FLIP, the federal Local Initiatives Program, which is in addition to the regular budget for small craft harbours. He also mentioned LIP, and he questioned whether LIP should become involved in the building of harbours, breakwaters and other port facilities. That is a good idea. The criticism I have been hearing over the years-I do not know if it is the same as the hon. member has been getting-is that the budget is allocated, tenders are called, and contracts are let to contractors outside the community who have their own permanent work force which they keep on month after month throughout the construction season. They bring this work force into a community and they build a structure. The structure is there for the community, but very little employment is created in that community in the building of that structure.
I see LIP and, I hope, the Canada Works program when it gets into place-that kind of initiative in job creation-as a very important step not only in designing and building these necessary facilities in the communities but in involving the people in those communities in the design, in the location and
in the actual construction. There is a real effort to be made in job creation, and it has been done under LIP. I hope that the principle can be followed and applied when the Canada Works Program is designed. I think it is a good thing, and I think the people in the community think it is a good thing. Those people who criticize it and abuse it should see some of the projects which have gone on in my constituency and which have been of enormous benefit to the fishermen and to other people in that kind of community.
I could go on to ask what more needs to be done. I think this is a good bill, and I think it is very necessary. As far as I am concerned, one of the most important aspects of it is the management capability which it gives to the minister. One real difficulty with regard to the operation of harbour and port facilities, and particularly wharves, has been the whole wharfinger system, and this applies not so much to the Department of Fisheries as it does to M.O.T. We have not been paying them enough.
We have not been making it attractive for people to become managers in those communities, and as a result not only are the harbours not well managed but, in fact, the freight which comes into them and goes out of them is spoiled and poorly handled in many ways. I think one of the most important things here is the clause regarding harbour management. We are looking for an improved system of harbour management, with trained harbour managers who have responsibility, enforcement authority, and adequate remuneration. That may be a small thing, but little things mean a lot, and if we can do something along that line alone, we will do a lot to improve our harbour facilities.
We need to rationalize community stages. The hon. member for St. John's West brought that up, but that control is now passing, as I understand it, from the federal government to the provincial government. I do not know what is happening, but I have not seen very much in terms of a definitive policy with regard to the upgrading and development of community stages. That needs to be done in conjunction with the building of wharves and breakwaters.
This bill is a good thing for the inshore fishery, as far as I am concerned. It follows a number of other initiatives this government has put into place with regard to the fishery. Earlier I talked about the price support program. There are fishermen in my riding who are making as much as $5,000 or $6,000 per year by way of income support through the price support program the minister has instituted, and that is a good thing.
The Salt Fish Corporation, another creation of this government, is doing a fantastic job in terms of the buying, processing and selling of fishermen's catches in areas where nobody else will do these things. The sin in Newfoundland is that there are still areas where fish are being thrown overboard, basically because nobody will buy them, and we need a rationalization of the fishplant operation in our province, but in the meantime and until such time as private enterprise either will, is made to,

December 10, 1976

or is given the incentive to get into these areas it is not into now, I think the Salt Fish Corporation is doing an excellent job. We need to rationalize our catching capacity, we need to improve our buying methods and, as I said before, we need to give as much protection as we can to the inshore fishery.
This is a little bit off the topic, but not entirely. We have to protect the inshore Fishermen from the offshore fishermen, and not just from the draggers and trawlers, but in some cases to protect the trap fishermen from the longliners. That kind of regulation has to be put in place applying to specific harbours and ports, and it is still not in place certainly in many places in my constituency right now and in other places in my province.
I wanted to make these few remarks on this bill and to congratulate the minister for bringing it in. 1 wanted to congratulate him also on the general job he is doing and the job that he seems to be doing in Newfoundland. I do not need to say this because it is well known in the province. There is an optimism among fishermen in Newfoundland for the first time in a long time. When I was in my riding this fall, this was plainly evident to me. In this past year the fishery in Newfoundland was possibly the only bright spot in the province, and I can only hope that this will continue to be the case.
Newfoundland is a fishing province and will continue to be a fishing province. It will continue to be primarily dependent on the fishery, and from a psychological point of view, if nothing else, I think this spirit of optimism now among the fishermen is a good thing and is something we have to encourage. Young people are now going into the fishery for the first time in a long time. In many cases they are being driven to it because of things like the close down at Come-By-Chance, the close down at Gull Island and the close down at Labrador Linerboard. The hon. member for St. John's West is well aware of these things, but it is an ill wind that blows nobody any good, and possibly the salutory thing which has come about because of these close downs is the fact that more people are turning to the fishery. In the long term I think that our economic base has to be designed with that particular industry in mind, so in that sense I say again that it is an ill wind that blows nobody any good.
There are those in my province who will say that the federal government has not kept faith with Newfoundland and Labrador, but this bill and this minister give the lie to those arguments. Although this bill is not major in proportions, it is another indication that in terms of fisheries certainly this government has kept faith with Newfoundland.
I would like to close by giving the minister the traditional Newfoundland toast, "Long may your big jib draw".

The wharves of many of the fishing harbours throughout my constituency were constructed by the Department of Public Works, but there was never any maintenance work carried out on them. They were constructed and just left to rot. Many of them, of course, were constructed right at election time, or their construction was promised at election time. That is similar to what is happening right now.
With regard to expenditures for fishing harbours and recreational harbours across Canada, I would like to refer to the year 1973-74. At that time in the province of Manitoba there were expenditures of $18,879. In 1974-75, an election year, there were expenditures of $357,200. In 1975-76 expenditures dropped to $215,200. We were not very good to this Liberal government in 1974 and did not send any new Liberal members to this House.
Of course we have to compare this with Quebec. I can be called bigoted if you like, but in 1973-74 Quebec received $887,000, in 1974-75, $4,361,000, and in 1975-76, the grand total of $10 million. They were certainly rewarded for voting the right way in 1974, Mr. Speaker. These are the figures I have in front of me and maybe in committee we will get down to the reason figures like this were used. I brought this matter up in the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and asked why $67 million was being spent on community affairs in Quebec in a particular year, and of course I was severely reprimanded by the minister. However, it took some real scratching to justify that amount being spent in one province while other provinces received less than half a million dollars. This shows what is happening across Canada, Mr. Speaker.
The fishing industry, recreational facilities, the small harbours in places in Manitoba where there are fish landings, the

December 10, 1976
Fishing and Recreational Harbours freshwater inland fishery in Lake Winnipeg and Lake Manitoba, are all vital to the economy of the province.
When the Department of Public Works transferred this mess to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) several of the wharves were already condemned and were a hazard to the area. Of course no funds are available now. Many of the residents of the area have brought this to the attention of various government officials, asking who is going to dismantle and clean up the mess created by the Department of Public Works. The new department claims it did not create the mess and cannot have anything to do with it. And so it goes around and around. It is really just a place for the polar bears.
There are harbour and wharf facilities at the Port of Churchill, but it is also a large recreational area. The Port of Churchill has some of the most exotic birds in Canada and people come to see them. We have a fort, the Prince of Wales, which took 40 years to construct. There is a conflict of interest, however, because the National Harbours Board owns the port but will not let anyone use the wharf for landing if they are taking tourists across to the other side to the fort to see part of the history of Canada and Manitoba. In many areas there should be joint use of the facilities.
In Manitoba, however, the facilities, being funded by the federal government, are minimum. Earlier I mentioned the figure $215,000. Mr. Speaker, that is not even one third of what it costs the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to fly to his constituency in the course of a few months. Our fishermen require facilities in order to land their fish at wharves along the lake front. Wharves were constructed over the years at places like Gull Harbour, Warrens Landing, George's Island, Grand Rapids, Dauphin River, Moose Lake and Le Pas. I could go on and on. These wharves were constructed by the government, and the fishermen understood that they would be maintained by the government. But today the fishermen, who are not receiving a decent price for their fish, have to maintain the wharves at their own expense. The whole set-up is false. The government comes in and spends plenty of money, and then tells the community that it has to maintain the facilities, and indeed many times the facilities are just too luxurious for the needs of the community.
It amazes me to hear members from the west coast speak of water transportation as being vitally important there. It is just as important in other parts of the country, Mr. Speaker. Water routes are the highways of the north because many areas in the north do not have roads. People depend on water when they travel, so they must have adequate facilities and protection when they dock their boats and unload their produce. There must be anchorage and fuel available. At the moment things are just like they are with railway transportation-no one seems to be interested in serving the north. They are interested in taking resources out of the north, but to get this government to put anything back in is a bit like trying to pull a hen's teeth, unless it foresees a big return.
May I call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD DAY MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AS LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
that Bill C-211, respecting Sir John A. Macdonald Day, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I consider myself very lucky to have drawn prime time on the last two Friday afternoons. Many of my colleagues know that this is for me an old subject. They are all kind enough, however, not to say it is just an old man dealing with an old subject. Whatever they think, they do not express it that way.
In universities they used to, and I trust still do occasionally, celebrate once a year an event called "Founder's Day". I suppose the presentation of my bill for many, many years is a sort of extension into parliament of the concept of founder's day.
I would have withdrawn this particular bill and indeed once did, on the understanding that the excellent and useful compromise of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs would have combined my immortalization of Sir John A. Macdonald and the reference of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), to Heritage Day, and the reference of an hon. member from British Columbia to our native peoples, into a heritage day. This day was to celebrate a particular person or event in the national heritage. It was an excellent idea. I was pleased with the manner in which the

December 10, 1976

committee at that time brought about a really good compromise, which I think is an expression of parliament at its best.
People in our society who denigrate the concept of compromise think, generally speaking, that to compromise is to err or sin. Edmund Burke did not think so. He said that all governments, indeed every human benefit and enjoyment, every virtue and prudent act, are founded on compromise and barter.
I regret that the government has chosen to cast aside the excellent work of the committee and the compromise reached by the members and proponents of other bills. We are now told that the Heritage Day act or bill will be brought in by the government. Nobody has said when. That is not a good thing.
I have watched for many years private members bringing forward suggestions and bills which, when eventually accepted, have been over-ridden by the government. In such cases the government has decided to bring in an act. That, I suggest, is a denigration of the private member. As I look at the flag on your right, Sir, I think of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), who for many years had a private bill on the order paper for introducing into our Chamber our nation's flag. He also proposed, year after year, private members' bills for honouring our former Prime Ministers by putting their pictures on the paper currency of our realm. He may have drawn some satisfaction from having his suggestion adopted by the House, even though he was pre-empted. Mr. Speaker, I thought it was not a good thing. I think the government denigrates members of parliament when it over-rides the consensus which was wisely arrived at by that committee headed, if my memory serves me correctly, by the distinguished man who is now the Speaker of our House.
While I would gladly have withdrawn this measure if the Heritage Day concept had been accepted in a spirit of decent and honourable compromise, I assure you, Sir, and my colleagues, that I have no apology for bringing forward this subject today. Indeed I doubt if there ever was a time when we could and should more appropriately stop to consider the values, virtues, and verities of our Founding Fathers, chief of whom was Sir John A. Macdonald, whose name is mentioned in the bill I am proposing.
I have said many times in this honourable Chamber that there is no immutable law which decrees that the great century-old dominion created by Macdonald and his colleagues from the Macdonald party and others will stay together or remain in the form which our wise Founding Fathers created. We know, as they knew, that the pressures for division, for separation, have always been stronger than the pressures for cohesion. Indeed, political scientists have always held that the greatest challenge in the Dominion of Canada was to make sure that the force which kept the country together should be stronger than the centrifugal force which would cause the parts to fly apart and go into separate orbits. If that were to happen it would destroy and deny that which the Fathers of Confederation had created.
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
This year, 1976, did not bring the first attempt to alter the union or to have one part of the country leave it. New Brunswick was probably the first separatist province, because it voted to stay out of Confederation before 1867. Nova Scotia came close thereafter, because in the year of Confederation, 1867, the people of Nova Scotia sent to this House 19 members, only one of whom was committed to Confederation. All the rest came here to break the pact of Confederation. On the same day Nova Scotia elected 38 members to its legislature; of those, two believed in Confederation; the others were totally against it. Providence decreed that one of those two should die before he could take his place in the assembly.
Prince Edward Island, that persevering, stubborn little area, then as now said no as long as it could, and until 1873 stayed out of the union. Newfoundland stayed out until 1949. Premier Fielding in 1886 won election in Nova Scotia on his program of being against Confederation and willingness to take Nova Scotia out of it. Ten years later that same hon. gentleman sat yonder, in the seats opposite me, as minister of finance for the Dominion Prime Minister, the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
In reciting these early events, in speaking about Sir John A. Macdonald, our Founding Father, I am not downplaying the seriousness of today's problems or the gravity of today's crisis.
I have never belonged to the "sky is falling" group, but I am somewhat amazed at the insousiance and casual response of many people in high places, and I speak with great candour because I include some members of this House, regarding current events and the change of government in Quebec. Of course the electorate of that province exercised its democratic right in deposing what it regarded as an inefficient and corrupt government. The Premier of Quebec, Mr. Levesque, has been consistently candid in expressing his view as to the best course of action for the people of Quebec. Mr. Parizeau showed the same candour when he was in Ottawa a few days ago. Hearing it suggested that the group of fiance ministers were the "new fathers of confederation," Mr. Parizeau said, I thought with extreme honesty "It might be more appropriate to call us fathers of de confederation."
In the face of all this I am amazed at that comfortable myopia afflicting people both at national and provincial levels, by that attitude which oozes a business as usual confidence. I read what provincial ministers said when they went back; 1 read what ministers said in this House, and I was amazed that they were not aware that we had entered a new and crucial chapter in our history. I must exclude the Premier of Newfoundland who spoke the day before yesterday in Toronto, I think, with what I would call anguished realism. Sir, things are not as usual. They are not as they were a few weeks ago.
Sir John A. Macdonald possessed many qualities. Surely one of the essential qualities of a nation-builder, of a statesman, is the quality of realism. He had no capacity to put before his eyes the blinkers of non-comprehension. He saw dangers and dealt with them skilfully and wisely. He dealt with them skilfully and wisely, never precipitously, but never did he hesitate to look upon a situation which endangered the union of which he was so much the founder.

December 10, 1976
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
There is much we could talk about in the bill asking this nation and this parliament to honour our first Prime Minister. There are many of the qualities I discussed before and other hon. members have discussed. I will mention only two things that strike me very much as being in the forefront in the mind of any Canadian who truly wishes to honour Sir John. A. Macdonald by following his example and seeking from his life, his career, his beliefs, something of value for today.
The first of these truly is that John A. Macdonald believed in a strong central government. In my opinion, he rightly divined the essential truth of confederation, that the whole is more important than the parts and, much more significant, is more important than the sum of the parts. Without that essential truth, there is little to be gained by talking much further about the "Dominion of the North," to use Professor Creighton's magnificent expression.
If today in response to the anxieties of the people of Quebec, and they rightfully have those anxieties and are expressing them in a very meaningful way, we so weaken the federal structure and so exalt the provincial entities as to have nothing more than a loose alliance of quasi-sovereign states, then we have in a little more than a century after his time destroyed Macdonald's work just as painfully and inevitably, as by decimating the federation.
The answer to our dilemma is not an easy one. However, I think we can all agree that whatever answers are vital, realistic and appropriate, that the one which should be excluded from any consideration is the balkanization of the country which John A. Macdonald, George Brown, Galt, Tilley and many others created for us. In my opinion, that is the way to the total loss of all that made us a great country on this continent.
My second and last extract from what I believe to be the verities of Sir John A. Macdonald's political philosophy and the realities of his political career is something else. This is even more dangerous than that which I have discussed. That is that in a country made up of many parts and different people, that any group-religious, racial, political, geographical or regional-should ever allow itself to become so brittle, bigoted, narrow or intolerant as to make it painful for different groups, classes or regions to remain comfortably in union with others.
John A. Macdonald was a very, very realistic man, not given much to talking about religion or piety. Certainly he never preached. However, he once said to someone in what is now called Quebec, and 1 quote:
The trouble is that you British Canadians can never forget that you were once supreme, that John Baptiste was once your hewer of wood and drawer of water. You struggle for ascendancy. If a lower Canadian Britisher desires to conquer he must stoop to conquer. He must make friends with the French without sacrificing the principles of his race or lineage. He must respect their nationality. Treat them as a nation; and they will act as a free people generally do-generously. Treat them as a faction and they will become factious.
Dr. Lower, once a great professor of mine, one of the great inspirers I had in my university days-not a P.C. fan-wrote of Macdonald, and I quote:
His stand with respect to the race question was consistent throughout his life whatever the cost to himself... he refused to raise the race cry at a time when he was in low political water.
This is the man I would seek that we honour. In this spirit I call on my colleagues to agree to salute the founder of our country. By renewing our faith in his broad-minded, tolerant, wise and sensible Canadianism, we may buttress the great nation which he and his associates bequeathed to us over a century ago.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD DAY MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AS LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always pleased to take part in private members' hour because if hon. members had more such hours, the country's business would often progress more rapidly.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for introducing Bill C-211 which commemorates one of the great and famous Canadians, Sir John A. Macdonald. In my opinion, the member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) would eventually be one of the best curators of museums in Canada and he would also be an excellent cultural affairs minister because I know that he is an intellectual who is always searching for historic papers unknown to most members who are busily dealing with more practical and earthly matters which are sterile and often prematurely bring death.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the introduction of the bill is timely. However I do not think the commemoration should be on January 10 because it is too cold at that time of the year. Still if he was the unifier of Canada, it should be a lesson for our Progressive Conservative friends who should study in depth the history of Canada, especially the achievements of Sir John A. Macdonald because when he realized that Canada could no longer survive, he suggested unification. To do so, he had to create a political party and to achieve that unity, he had to have the services of another famous Canadian, namely Sir Georges-fitienne Cartier.
I think this is a lesson for today's Progressive Conservative members and for all politicians. We must refrain from trying to divide this country through all kinds of speeches which basically are made only in an effort to get some publicity. And by that I do not suggest that many members of this House would have to be commended for keeping silent since they would have taken one of the best opportunities not to say anything rather than speak nonsense. This is how we will be able to better understand the inequalities which exist in Canada and to promote some unity. The great dream of Sir John A. Macdonald was to unify Canada from sea to sea.
Of course, he was not perfect and even had vices. But he had qualities, great talent and above all, he was a great visionary. I think he is an example for all of us in 1976, given the events which are now taking place in Canada. Last night the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) gave a lecture to some students, and I understand he said that if Quebec decides to separate, western Canada would want to do the same. This is

December 10, 1976

hardly the way to materialize Sir John A. Macdonald's dream for Canada. Hon. members should take one or two hours each week to speak about the qualities, the defects, but especially the greatness and achievements of great Canadian politicians. And God knows there were quite a few! I congratulate the hon. member for Hillsborough for moving this bill which gives a deeper meaning to Canadian nationalism. A feeling which has never existed in Canada is love for one's country, pride to belong to Canada. Some provinces no longer even teach Canada's history these days. It is a shame! I think the federal government will have to do its best so that free textbooks of Canadian history be distributed throughout the country, in the west and in the east, and that all Canadians know what happened since Confederation. There have been too many different versions of Canadian history, very often biased, and we should have one which would inform people, especially the young. And I think that if we do not do this, the dismemberment of the country is possible.
It is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, after only a hundred years of Confederation, for some members of this House, seeking political gain or publicity, to advocate the dismemberment of Canada. I was happily surprised to see that the life of Sir John A. Macdonald had only one goal, the unification of Canada. He saw Canada, that big continent, divided into many small territories.
He knew we could not survive that way as a nation. Then there was the American border incident, when he became the apologist of those who invaded us: the Americans. It is Sir John A. Macdonald who defended their cause. He was not lucky, one of them was sentenced to die, and the others at least survived, but this gave him the idea that Canada should get together in case the United States decided to invade Canada. This is how the idea of getting the other colonies, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, both Lower and Higher Canadas together, crossed his mind.
Let it be a lesson for all of us. The House should consider more bills similar to that introduced by the hon. member for Hillsborough. Mr. Speaker, I know that a number of hon. members want to make a number of historic points concerning this. Although $5 bills carry the picture of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, it is no reason to assume that, just because $10 bills carry that of Sir John A. Macdonald, that one John A. Macdonald is worth two Lauriers. It only means that the decisions had nothing to do with history.
A $50 bill bears the effigy of Mackenzie King and a $100 bill bears that of Borden. This does not mean that two Kings equal one Borden. I think that things are equal and that we should not make any difference between hon. members, be they Progressive Conservatives, Liberals or New Democrats. We are here to take all the little steps that create a nation and the philosophical or theoretical speeches from hon. members, ministers or senators do not promote a nation very much. To my mind, we can build that new nation during the private members' hour. We must work hard so that tomorrow our nation will be stronger than that which existed more than 100
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
years ago. Long ago, we had great men who attempted to create unity once for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with others who have or will yet take part in this debate in thanking the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for introducing this bill again so that we can have this discussion about the great heritage which is ours as Canadians.
I believe it appropriate that the hon. member for Hillsborough should give us the dissertation he did about the contribution made to our national life by Sir John A. Macdonald. I am sure we all agree as well that the statement just made by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) helps to emphasize the fact that ours is a multi-heritage. It means a great deal to us that we have this kind of country. Anything we can do to enrich the quality of life we already enjoy because of the varied strains in our national fabric is to be encouraged, and it is good to reflect that in this place we turn our backs on bigotry and dissension, and do everything we can to achieve a united Canada.
I must say 1 differ slightly from the hon. member for Hillsborough on just one point. He expressed some concern that the outcome of today's discussion might be a bill brought in by the government rather than the passing of a bill brought in by a private member. I hope it does not sound like the boasting that I suppose it is for me to say that I have had the privilege of bringing in quite a number of private members' bills and resolutions which were never passed, but the ideas of which have been taken over and can now be found in our labour legislation, in our pension and social security legislation, and in one or two other places as well. What counts is the legislation, not whose name is on it. To me, Mr. Speaker, that is the purpose of private members' hour. We have the opportunity to present ideas, and if they have merit they become popular and are in due course accepted.
So I am glad that there is a reasonably good prospect that the idea of a holiday in Canada's mid-winter, to be known as Heritage Day, will soon become something which is on our statute books. One of the members who has contributed very effectively to this is the hon. member for Hillsborough. If we do come out of this with a Heritage Day, one of the reasons that it will have that name is that members like the hon. member for Hillsborough pressed the point that we should reflect upon what has been done for our country by men like Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and even some of those of more recent days whom we remember.
The government has been very precise in its promise that we are going to get legislation along this line this session. Instead of our being given one bill establishing Heritage Day in February it is going to be one of those omnibus bills which this government is famous for, which puts all of the national

December 10, 1976
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
holidays into one piece of legislation. I hope it will be quite a few; the more the merrier.
I hope there are not too many tricks in the bill that will cause its debate to be extended. As a matter of fact the committee to which the hon. member for Hillsborough referred made the compromise suggestion so long ago that we have already missed two of the Heritage Days in February that we could have had if the bill that came back from that standing committee had been passed. The reason I keep popping up on Thursdays during the time we discuss House business, and on every other possible occasion, to try to press the government to bring in its holidays bill is that things can drag on around here and get lost. I know that February may be a couple of months away, but unless we get the holidays bill soon and pass it, we will have a third February without a Heritage Day, despite the fact that the committee unanimously recommended it some time ago.
That, Mr. Speaker, is mainly what I wanted to say. I appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Hillsborough that his particular bill may not be passed, but he has made real input into the legislation which will come. It will be a Heritage Day, the new day that is going to be added, so that we can reflect from year to year on various aspects of our heritage, one of them being the contribution made to this country by the first Prime Minister of Canada.
I just plead again that the government not stall any longer. The last couple of times I have asked the government House leader for the introduction of this bill he has come back with some notion about not being sure whether it would be passed quickly. How does he know until he files the bill, lets it have first reading, and gives the House a chance to debate it? I believe that the House will accept the bill rather quickly, especially when we see February coming close.
I think it is useful to have this debate this afternoon, not only for the purpose of pushing the government to act on its holidays bill, which will include Heritage Day, but so that we can express again our desire to have that kind of day in Canada's calendar.
I have just one other point which is a bit personal, Mr. Speaker. I was delighted to hear the hon. member for Hillsborough quote words about Sir John A. Macdonald used by Dr. Arthur Lower. He happens to be an old friend of mine from his Winnipeg days, and like my hon. friend I think he is one of the great Canadians of this century. His book "From Colony to Nation" stands out as a tremendous piece of Canadian history, and his book of a decade ago entitled "My First 75 Years" is a delightful volume. I hope that the time will come when Dr. Lower will be able to write a book on his first 100 years.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is good to have this discussion this afternoon, and I earnestly hope that the government will file very soon its bill which will include Heritage Day, so it can be in effect by February 1977.

It was precisely because there were these various ideas that the committee thought that a happy compromise would be to pick a day which was not any one of them on which, by order in council, the decision could be made each year as to which aspect of our heritage to celebrate. Some of these aspects would involve persons, and one aspect that was part of that thinking was the heritage of our national flag. I do not think my hon. friend and I should hold up the decision on this matter by worrying about the date. February 15 is a good day. It is the day after St. Valentine's day, and some members suggested that.
Our national flag is one aspect of our heritage upon which we could reflect, and I believe it would be covered in the provisions for Heritage Day. The important thing is not the precise day but to have a day that covers all aspects of our heritage, and I think most Canadians would also like the idea of a holiday in mid-winter.

subtopic: SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD DAY MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AS LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to join with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in support for his Bill C-211, respecting Sir John A. Macdonald day, and to speak on it not in terms of a Heritage Day, or a national flag day-although
December 10, 1976

those aspects of it might well be in a sense brought in, depending on the day on which it fell- but rather in terms of Sir John A. Macdonald as the first Prime Minister of a confederated, independent Canada, so that we can remember the ranking Father of Confederation among all those visionary people who saw the value of a united nation and who looked beyond that to the possibility of a dominion from sea to sea, as Canada now is, and which I know hon. members join me in saying will be for a long time to come.
One of our problems in this country is that we have been slow to do things about our symbols, whether it has been a national flag, which we finally obtained through great turmoil, concern and agitation, or a national anthem, which we have not yet achieved. That is one of my concerns, having worked on the committee dealing with the question in my first term in parliament, coming back so many years later to find that we are no further ahead on that than we were then. Finally we have been slow in respect of the symbolic designation of a Sir John A. Macdonald Day to honour that founding Father of Confederation who first led this country.
Every independent nation, particularly on this continent, tends to honour the first, whether it be the president or, in our case, the Prime Minister-the first leader of the country. In doing that I think we would be doing something for national unity. We must remember that Sir John was a member of the Parliament of Canada in pre-confederation days, in the days when it met at Montreal. He was not a part of the sad events that led to the destruction of those parliament buildings and the eventual removal of parliament from Montreal to this location.
One cannot undo history, but it has always seemed to me that our chances for a unified Canada at this point would have been much greater if the national capital had remained in that great city of Montreal, of which I am very fond, and which is part and parcel of the united Canada that is mine and the heritage, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will have it, of all Canadians.
There is one thing about Sir John A. Macdonald that touches the heart of any member from British Columbia, and that is that he represented a constituency in British Columbia for some years. In those days elections were conducted a little differently and it was possible to stand for more than one constituency. In 1878 Sir John had a choice after the election dust had settled. He had been elected in two places, Marquette, Manitoba, and Victoria, British Columbia. As the great biographer Donald Creighton said, the choice was pleasantly easy. I am sure that a choice between that city on the Pacific coast and a city in almost any other part of Canada would have been an easy choice. Sir John represented Victoria.
Of course we know, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows, that our province has continued in the tradition of welcoming people who have been defeated elsewhere and looked to British Columbia as a possible place for continued representation. We have a rather lengthy history,
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
and I think it is an honourable and important one, of sending distinguished people to this Chamber when it seems to be necessary to follow that route. I do not know whether sometime in the future we might even have the honour of sending the present member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) back here, but I think we would probably find it in our generous hearts in British Columbia to consider that as well.
Sir John A. later took an epic journey through the constituency that I represent, accompanied by his wife Agnes, and was so struck by the beauty of the mountains through which they were passing he rode for some time on the cow-catcher of the train which was carrying them to the coast on that great run commemorating the completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Again Creighton waxed eloquently when he said:
They travelled through Rogers Pass and past Craigellachie on the buffer bar; from it they watched the great coiling valleys of the Thompson and Fraser Rivers.
Again sometimes I think we should, as well as being concerned about the history of our country on afternoons like this, be also concerned about the geography of it, because I cannot believe it in my heart that the majority of the people in my province of Canada would want to remove from the country the Rocky Mountains and that great geography beyond to the west, any more than any province would find it in the hearts of the majority of the people to remove the great city of Montreal, the great St. Lawrence River, or the mountains to the north from Canada. We are a country, and surely the glory of being a Canadian is the glory of not only the history but the geography of this vast land of ours, and any proposal that diminishes it concerns me very much, and makes the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough even more pertinent as we debate and discuss our future as a country in these somewhat difficult times.
It seems to me entirely appropriate that we should be prepared to designate a day as Sir John A. Macdonald Day. Whether that takes the form of a national holiday at the moment is not that important, but I would feel its contribution toward national unity would be greater than designating the same day as Heritage Day, when I am afraid the very nature of the term would lead us to celebrate such a variety and multitude of aspects of our heritage that the concentration on national unity could well be less.
In Sir John A. Macdonald we had a man of wit, wisdom, and ability, and yet as one praises the virtues of that great figure one should always remember too his basic humanity, that he had frailties and weaknesses which he overcame, and the overcoming of those, I think, led to the ability that enabled him to form the kind of partnership that formed Canada. We must realize that he, through partnership particularly with Georges Etienne Cartier, was able to persuade the other parts of Canada that came into Confederation that this was a lasting nation that had room in it for the French-speaking part, the English-speaking part, and any other part that found its way in. That appeal reached my province of British Columbia whose unity as a colony predates Confederation. British Columbia had a choice in the years prior to 1871 as to how its

December 10, 1976
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
future would be developed. It chose to throw its lot in with Canada.
I know there are people in my province and in others who now consider western separatism as an alternative. I do not for a moment, and I always found when talking to young Canadians during my days teaching school that when you asked them whether they saw themselves as British Columbians or as Canadians first, when they thought about it, they said they were Canadians. They realized that the unity of Confederation had worked for them and that their country was a larger thing than just that area of the Rockies and west.
I am happy to join in supporting this bill because I think we have not had a time so propitious for marking the beginnings of this country, beginnings that were designed well, put together in strength, and built to last.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief, but I did not want to let this opportunity go by without saying a few words about this bill introduced by the hon. member for Hillsborough (M. Macquarrie). I am convinced that if the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) could have been in the House for the debate on this bill, he would certainly have had very interesting things to say because he is a genuine Canadian. He said so and made it his way of life. I am also convinced that he knows by heart the history of Canada and the great men who founded and administered our country.
When I was in school I always strongly wanted to know and discover more about Canada, its beginnings, how men at that time worked to build a great country and unite all parts of a great continent, as was so appropriately pointed out earlier by the sponsor of this bill whom I congratulate wholeheartedly.
We cannot say this is an omnibus bill because it is very clear. And since I like clear legislation, I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member. He has expressed his views in a few lines but there are many things in them.
Some time ago, when I introduced a similar bill in the House, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Les lies (Mr. Bech-ard) chided me for not spending much time on the preparation of my bill. Of course he was only teasing me, but that shows once more that hon. members favour bills which deal with separate subjects.

Mr. Speaker, that is a good point. I agree with the comment of the hon. member. I will try too remember that.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the comments of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) since he recognized, on behalf of French Canadians, that we are very happy to honour a man who was so far-sighted. This is why in my opinion we should immediately accept the suggestion made in this bill and chose a day to show our gratitude towards a great Canadian.
In view of the present situation and the ideas which now prevail in our country, it would be a good thing to show the young generation, to show our children what exactly is Canada, to tell of its beginning, its history, its difficulties, because there were problems at the time of Confederation and even before that. The present means of communication did not exist at the time. Today, the Prime Minister of Canada can call a conference of provincial premiers within 24 hours. It was not possible at that time because of transportation and communication problems. However they understood each other and achieved a wonderful objective. This is why the present generation should know the true history of our country instead of a fake history inspired by a spirit of revenge because of won or lost battles. If the) knew our true history they would feel more patriotic and love their country.
I always understood that my motherland begins where I first lived as a child. Then, gradually I understood that motherland is the whole territory where we live. Then our motherland is Canada. Like everybody I hope that our country will continue to grow and develop. We are surely right to be inspired by the high aspirations of Sir John A. Macdonald and by commemorating this great Canadians by a special day in his honour we could succeed in making Canadians of today aware of those very important events.
Mr. Speaker, I am referring to the history of Louis Riel. I do not want to prolong the debate and I congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) who just made a wise suggestion. I wanted to say in a few words that I support this legislation and that I am looking forward to see its proposals come into effect.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it can well be said that the hon. members who have spoken before me have carried with them some truly impressive reasons and truly impressive backgrounds, such as that in philosophy of the mover of the motion. I do not have such a background. I do not have a PhD., an MD., or any of the letters that many people find important in this world. But I do have three letters that I think are the most important that a person in this country can ever put beside his name. Those letters are Cdn., the short form for Canadian.
